posts.title: You own it.
posts.caption:
You own it. That’s the idea shaping Wahoo.

We’re developing a jetboard with serviceability and long-term ownership in mind. Understand it. Maintain it. Make it yours.

These are design ambitions as we develop the board.

Approved concept image of a jetboard from above in dark water, with the words Understand it. Knowledge is part of ownership. Marked Concept visual, development ambition. Card 2 of 5.

posts.title: One board. Many minds.
posts.caption:
One board. Many minds.

Ten defined AI roles help investigate Wahoo’s development. Leo connects the work, specialists explore questions, and Isaac challenges consequential conclusions. Max decides what moves forward.

The team works on demand. Physical tests are still needed to validate the board.

posts.title: Inside the simulator.
posts.caption:
Start with movement. Then ask what happens to pressure, heat and waves.

Wahoo’s simulator grows through small, checkable models. These saved schematics and synthetic benchmarks help us test the software before making engine predictions.

They are development tools, not measured engine performance.

cards.alt: Pale poster titled Start with movement. Exact existing 2D piston, rod and crank schematic at its saved 90-degree pose stands to the right of the supporting text: One step toward a model we can question. Label: Saved 2D schematic, not to scale. Card 1 of 5.

Graphite poster titled Less volume. More pressure. Original saved pressure versus volume compression curve, with original axes, units and labels. Compression runs right to left. Synthetic closed-mass adiabatic ideal-gas qualification fixture with no heat input; not a measured Wahoo trace. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster titled Add heat. Check the change. Original synthetic temperature versus time curves show prescribed heating and cooling at fixed mass and volume. Original units and legends retained. No wall-cooling correlation solved. Card 3 of 5.

Graphite poster with a large saved pressure-history plot above the headline Follow the pulse. Exact original axes, sample curves, units and receiver legends are preserved for a stationary uniform linear-acoustic rigid-boundary benchmark. Text: A saved benchmark. One bounded physics question. Not nonlinear exhaust blowdown. Card 4 of 5.

Graphite poster with original Wahoo wordmark, titled What does the model keep? Existing acoustic energy benchmark plot retains units, samples and labels. Text: Energy is part of the check. Engine performance still needs validation. Solid curve: rigid termination retains pulse energy. Dashed curve: absorbing termination lets energy leave. Not a dyno result. Card 5 of 5.

posts.title: Hull development: look closer.
posts.caption:
Look closer.

Hull development means more than choosing a silhouette. We inspect surfaces, cut sections, follow profiles and mark questions for review. Then limited CFD cases explore the interaction with water.

These are geometry studies and early simulation evidence. They do not establish handling, stability or final performance; physical validation is still ahead.

cards.alt: Dark poster titled Look closer. Large crop of the existing native H0 R02 tail surface zebra inspection, with original Wahoo wordmark. Text: The shape behind the ride. Label: H0 R02, surface review, not water flow. Card 1 of 5.

Dark poster titled Slice through the question. Original overlaid transverse tail sections from the derived Brep preserve equal Y and Z scales, original units and station legend. The unchanged legend is enlarged separately below the plot so it no longer covers the curves. Text: The tail changes in three dimensions. Sections help us see how. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster titled Follow the shape. Existing source-derived Brep tail cutaway illustration shows transverse and longitudinal section curves and original C1/C4 witness labels. This is a clipped analytical view; the actual hull remains closed. Text: Sections and profiles. One three-dimensional question. Card 3 of 5.

Pale poster with original black Wahoo symbol. Text: Check the whole surface. A full underside board zebra-pattern image sits directly on the pale background with transparent surroundings. Text: Zebra patterns help us inspect surface continuity. Label: Native surface review, not water flow. Background-removed presentation derivative of the existing native review image, not new geometry or analysis. Card 4 of 5.

Dark poster titled Then ask the water. Actual saved historical CFD20 free-surface field at simulation time 1.579983709 seconds. Conditions printed on artwork: historical 20 km/h, bare board, no rider, closed intake, no jet thrust. Text: Early CFD explores a limited case. Physical testing is still ahead. Not performance validation. Card 5 of 5.

posts.title: Control. In your hand.
posts.caption:
Control in your hand. The design is still open.

We’re exploring how grip, throttle, starting and essential information could come together in one handheld controller. The blue-accent presentation concept introduces the idea; three other visual directions keep the housing and grip discussion open.

The intended features include a progressive trigger, thumb-operated rear starter, top display, left- or right-side lanyard positions, and separate grab-line and cable interfaces. Ergonomics, operation and safety functions still need testing. No final design has been selected.

Which visual direction would you explore—and what would matter most in your hand?

cards.alt: Pale Wahoo poster with original black shaded W symbol. Large words: Control. In your hand. The unchanged blue-accent tc04 handheld-controller concept sits to the right. Text: One interface. Four visual directions. The design stays open. Label: Presentation concept, no final design selected. Card 1 of 5.

Graphite poster headed Keep the grip. Reach the controls. The unchanged tc04 controller concept sits beside five intended functions: progressive trigger for throttle modulation; rear starter for thumb-operated starting; top display for essential operating information; left/right lanyard for stance-aware attachment positions; lower interfaces for grab line and control cable. Label: Design intent, ergonomics and function untested. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster showing the unchanged tc01 controller concept with open head, visible fasteners and textured grip. Headline: Open expression. Option 01. Original black shaded Wahoo symbol. Label: Visual direction, no final selection. Card 3 of 5.

Blue graphite poster showing the unchanged tc02 controller concept at large scale on the left. Headline: Fuller form. Option 02. Text: A fuller housing. Diagonal grip texture. Blue detailing. Original white Wahoo symbol. Label: Visual direction, no final selection. Card 4 of 5.

Pale poster showing the unchanged tc03 controller concept on the right. Headline: Smoother surfaces. Option 03. Text: A quieter housing treatment. A different grip texture. Question: Which direction would you explore? Original black Wahoo wordmark. Label: Concepts, ergonomics still to be tested. Card 5 of 5.

posts.title: Product / design story

cards.alt: A pale blue CAD-derived H0 R03 hull is rotated into a dramatic upright composition on a dark background. “A shape worth a closer look.” The complete hull remains visible. The original shaded white Wahoo W symbol sits at the lower left.
A large cropped detail of the native hull underside crosses a blue-grey background diagonally. “Follow the surface.” The crop is a detail of the approved render, not new geometry.
The native hull side profile sits above a large blue “Shape. Check. Refine.” headline. “Development in progress” qualifies the product stage.

posts.caption:
A shape is where the questions begin.

A perspective, a closer look underneath, then the side profile: three native CAD-derived views of the H0 R03 hull reference. Looking from different angles helps us question the design before making claims about how it will ride.

These are development views, not a finished production board or proof of handling. Which angle would you like to explore?

posts.title: Engineering made simple

cards.alt: “Motion before power.” Native partial-piston linework with schematic crank and rod appears on an open pale background. “Start with something we can check.” The original shaded black Wahoo W symbol sits at the lower right.

“A turn becomes a stroke.” The published simulator’s stronger two-dimensional cylinder, piston, crank and rod schematic is shown at its exact saved 90-degree pose. Schematic components and saved landmarks; not to scale, with no new model run.

“Back. And forth.” A blue curve shows all 361 exact saved nominal piston-pin positions in metres against crank angle from zero to 360 degrees. This is a software motion trace, not an engine performance plot.
“361 positions. One careful check.” A larger cropped native partial-piston linework detail sits above 361 dots. “Software correspondence. Physical validation ahead.”

“Confidence starts with the basics.” An unchanged native hull perspective connects the motion story back to the board being developed. “A development story. One verified step at a time.” The original shaded black Wahoo W symbol sits at the upper right.

posts.caption:
Does it move the way we expect?

The crank turns; the piston moves back and forth. Our nominal software/CAD check compared 361 saved positions. Checking that digital motion is one small step toward a product we can trust.

The linework shows partial source geometry with a schematic mechanism. It does not validate a complete engine, combustion, power, physical reliability or safety. Physical validation remains ahead.

What part of Wahoo would you like us to explain next?
